notes.1a: (i) There were many good answers to this question although some candidates unnecessarily repeated the question in their responses. Any explanation of an ionisation trend down a group should always refer to the changing size of the attraction between the nucleus and electrons, in terms of the changing distance and shielding. Some candidates responded that the distance and shielding effects resulted in less energy being needed to remove the outermost electron. As the question states that the ionisation energies decrease down the group there could be no credit for this.
notes.1aii: Once again, as a comparison of ionisation energies is involved, a key part of the answer must be a reference to the attraction from the nucleus. The most common mistake here was to refer to ‘orbitals’ or ‘sub-shells’ when the large difference between 2nd and 3rd ionisation energies here needs explaining in terms of the fact that the 3rd electron is in a shell closer to the nucleus than the first two electrons.
notes.1b: (i) A surprising number of candidates suggested that the outer configuration was 4d2 instead of 5s2.
notes.1bii: Many candidates were able to state correctly that the four peaks are due to the presence of four isotopes although many referred to isomers instead of isotopes. Many were not specific and did not state four.
notes.1c: (i) This was generally well answered although there was some inversion in the answers with candidates defining oxidation (loss of electrons) instead of defining an oxidising agent (an electron acceptor).
notes.1cii: This calculation was also generally well done although some candidates used the wrong atomic mass for Ba.
notes.1d: (i) A majority of candidates correctly identified X, Y and Z although there were quite a few who got MgO and Mg(OH) the wrong way round and others who gave incorrect formulae.
notes.1dii: Most candidates suggested nitric acid as the reagent needed but here, as in several other equation-based questions, balancing caused problems for many candidates.
notes.1iv: Several candidates suggested reactions of Mg with something other than water despite the labelling on the reaction scheme.
notes.2a: The equation was generally well done although balancing again caused some problems and some candidates thought that the formula of iron(III) oxide was FeO .
notes.2b: (i) Few candidates offered the key idea that the reaction is too exothermic though many earned credit with a reference to the production of an acid spray.
notes.2bii: This gave another example of the importance of reading the question carefully as the stem of (b) described this two-step process. However, many candidates did not provide two correct equations.
notes.2c: (i) Many candidates offered dot-and-cross diagrams, which are not required when the question is about the shape – but this may have been intended as an aid to working out if/how many lone pairs were present. A significant number of candidates incorrectly offered a linear shape for SO .
notes.2cii: Many candidates struggled with the recall of bond angles here.
notes.2d: (i) It was pleasing to see that so many candidates noted that there were four marks available for this answer as it led to a significant number of sufficiently detailed and well-explained responses. Some candidates confused the concepts of rate and equilibria and care must be taken to avoid suggesting that only the rate of the forward or reverse reaction increases when temperature is increased. Both rates increase when temperature is increased (i.e. the overall rate at which equilibrium is attained increases) but the position of equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction whenever temperature is increased.
notes.2dii: The most common problem encountered here was for candidates to include square brackets in their expressions. The use of square brackets specifically refers to concentration (in mol dm-3) so they should only be used when an expression is being written for K , not K . c p
notes.2iii: This proved to be one of the more challenging questions on the paper. As advised in previous examiner reports, the key in questions of this type is to remember that there are potentially three quantitative pieces of information about each species in the equation: initial amounts, final/equilibrium amounts and the amounts reacting or being produced. Crucially, the stoichiometric ratio shown in the equation only applies to the last of these. In this case the initial amounts of SO and O were given as 2.00 mol each, and the final/equilibrium amount of SO as 1.80 mol. From 2 3 this it can be deduced that 1.80 mol of SO has been produced during the reaction. As the ratio of SO :SO is 1:1, the amount of SO that has reacted must be the same meaning that 2.00 – 1.80 2 3 2 i.e. 0.20 mol will remain. The ratio of O :SO is, however, 1:2 meaning that, to produce a given 2 3 number of moles of SO , half that many moles of O need to react. In this case 0.90 mol of O will 3 2 2 react in order to produce 1.80 mol of SO meaning that 1.10 mol will remain in the equilibrium mixture. The next stage was to calculate mole fractions for each species followed by partial pressures before generating the final answer. Credit was available here for each stage of the calculation; candidates should be reminded that this is only possible for Examiners if all working is clearly shown.
notes.3a: The reaction between an alkene and hot, concentrated potassium manganate(VII) seems to be well known by most candidates although some struggled to apply the concept in this context. Candidates would benefit from more practice at correct representations of structural formulae as many were confusing. Candidates should be encouraged to use brackets to show, for example, H C=C(CH ) or H C=C(CH )CH rather than the incorrect H C=CCH CH although this was not 2 3 2 2 3 3 2 3 3 penalised.Candidates are strongly advised to include the double bond when drawing the structural formula of an alkene as it helps to ensure the correct number of carbon bonds in the structure and also removes ambiguity.
notes.3b: (i) The definition of stereoisomerism (as “molecules with the same molecular and structural formula but a different spatial arrangement of their atoms”) was not well known by candidates. Descriptions of structural isomerism or stereoisomerism were often incorrectly given.
notes.3bii: Candidates must be aware that the formal definition of a displayed formula is one that shows all atoms and bonds in a molecule. The commonest mistake made here was to abbreviate the CH groups instead of drawing them ‘displayed’. Candidates must also be aware that, when a question asks for the name of a compound, the full name is expected. In this case many candidates were not awarded credit as they labelled their structures as ‘cis’ and ‘trans’ without including ‘but-2-ene’.
notes.3c: Most candidates chose a suitable reducing agent but a significant minority offered a structure instead of the name of the product.
notes.4a: Candidates very often wrote an equation that was correct apart from balancing of the species.
notes.4b: (i) The vast majority of candidates recognised that this reaction was an oxidation.
notes.4bii: Following on from (i) candidates were then able to suggest a suitable oxidising agent. Many candidates did not specify ‘reflux’, which is necessary to ensure complete oxidation to the carboxylic acid as opposed to the intermediate aldehyde.
notes.4c: This proved to be one of the most difficult questions on the paper. Relatively few candidates were able to apply the idea of an acid reacting with a carbonate, into this organic context. Very few recognised that the formula of the salt produced would be (CH CH COO) Ca as the calcium ion 3 2 2 has a 2+ charge.
notes.4d: (i) This was generally well answered although some candidates did not specify that the sulfuric acid should be concentrated.
notes.key_messages:
Candidates are reminded to read questions carefully and check answers thoroughly. In this paper,
candidates would have benefitted from this particularly in Questions 1(d)(ii), 1(d)(iv), 2(b)(ii), 4(a) and 4(c),
where answers frequently included unbalanced equations or, in some cases, no equations at all.

notes.general_comments:
This paper tested a range of recall and application skills from across the AS syllabus and discriminated
effectively between all candidates. It did highlight, however, some syllabus areas with which candidates were
less familiar; specifically Group II chemistry, shapes of molecules and equilibrium-based calculations.
